messages.content: I want to develop a subsurface two-phase flow surrogate that preserves local mass conservation while generalizing across unseen permeability connectivity. The maximum cellwise mass-balance error needs to stay below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. On unseen channel connectivity, breakthrough-time error needs to remain below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver.

Those are two distinct requirements for the surrogate. It must keep the largest cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of the mass injected in each timestep, and it must predict breakthrough time on unseen channel connectivity with less than 5% error relative to a converged finite-volume solver. The first concerns local conservation; the second concerns predictive accuracy when connectivity is unfamiliar.
What does “local” add to the conservation requirement?

It makes the individual cell the level at which the mass-balance error matters. A small error after combining many cells would not, by itself, establish that every cell satisfies the requirement. The stated limit applies to the maximum cellwise error, so a single cell above the limit would matter even if errors elsewhere were small.
And the 0.1% is measured against injected mass per timestep, not against the mass in each cell?

Correct. The stated comparison is to injected mass per timestep. Expressed as a fraction, 0.1% is 0.001 of that timestep’s injected mass. The requirement does not replace that reference quantity with each cell’s mass.
Does “maximum” mean an average error below 0.1% would be enough?

No. An average could be below 0.1% while the largest cellwise mass-balance error exceeds it. The stated requirement is that the maximum cellwise error stay below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep, not merely that an average does.
I also want to be precise about the breakthrough condition. What is it being compared with?

The comparison is the breakthrough time from a converged finite-volume solver. On unseen channel connectivity, the surrogate’s breakthrough-time error must remain below 5% versus that solver result. The condition names both the evaluation setting and the comparison baseline.
Does “unseen” refer to channel connectivity rather than just another permeability value?

Yes—the requirement specifically says unseen channel connectivity. It asks for generalization when the connectivity represented by the permeability is unseen. It does not reduce that requirement to a claim about different permeability values with otherwise familiar connectivity.
Could a surrogate satisfy the mass-balance limit and still miss the breakthrough-time target?

Conceptually, yes. Keeping cellwise mass-balance error below its limit does not, on its own, establish that breakthrough time will be within 5% of the converged finite-volume result. The goal calls for both properties; neither numerical requirement stands in for the other.
And if breakthrough time is close to the solver result, that does not prove local conservation either?

Right. A close breakthrough-time comparison addresses the stated timing error on unseen channel connectivity. It does not establish the maximum cellwise mass-balance error. Both requirements have to be considered on their own terms.
Does the wording prescribe a particular way to build the surrogate?

No particular surrogate architecture or conservation mechanism is specified. The goal states what the subsurface two-phase flow surrogate should preserve and how its performance should be bounded, without selecting an implementation.
Because this is two-phase flow, does the 0.1% statement give separate numerical limits for each phase?

The stated requirement gives a maximum cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep, but it does not separately state a numerical threshold for each phase. It is important not to add a phase-specific limit that has not been specified.
Is the finite-volume solver described as the benchmark for the conservation limit too?

The explicit solver comparison belongs to the breakthrough-time requirement: below 5% error versus a converged finite-volume solver on unseen channel connectivity. The conservation requirement is stated as a cellwise mass-balance limit relative to injected mass per timestep, not as an error relative to that solver.
How strictly should I read “below” in the two thresholds?

As strict limits in the stated requirements: the maximum cellwise mass-balance error stays below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep, and breakthrough-time error remains below 5% versus the converged finite-volume solver on unseen channel connectivity. Neither is worded as “at or below.”
So the goal is not simply to get a plausible two-phase flow prediction. It has a local constraint and a generalization target.

Exactly. The surrogate is meant to represent subsurface two-phase flow while preserving local mass conservation, with the maximum cellwise mass-balance error below the specified per-timestep limit. It must also generalize across unseen permeability connectivity, with breakthrough-time error below the specified limit on unseen channel connectivity relative to the converged finite-volume solver. Those are targets for the surrogate, not claims that it has already met them.

For the subsurface two-phase flow surrogate, I propose training a transmissibility-aware graph network to predict phase fluxes and saturation increments, then projecting the predicted fluxes onto finite-volume continuity constraints.

That gives the surrogate two stages: a graph network makes predictions informed by transmissibility, and a projection adjusts the predicted phase fluxes to satisfy finite-volume continuity constraints. The network would predict both phase fluxes and saturation increments. The projection is specifically a step applied to the fluxes; the proposal does not say that it independently projects the saturation increments.
What does transmissibility awareness contribute to the proposal?

It means transmissibility is relevant to how the graph network predicts flow, rather than treating connections as interchangeable. That fits a goal involving permeability connectivity: the surrogate needs to respond to how flow paths connect. It is a description of what the network should be aware of, not a claim that it will generalize successfully to every unseen connectivity.
Why predict phase fluxes as well as saturation increments?

They describe related but different parts of a two-phase flow update. Phase fluxes describe phase transport between locations, while saturation increments describe changes in saturation. Predicting both gives the surrogate quantities associated with transport and with its evolving state. The proposal does not, by itself, specify exactly how those predictions are reconciled with one another.
Is the projection just another name for penalizing conservation error during training?

No. As stated, the proposal includes a subsequent projection of predicted fluxes onto finite-volume continuity constraints. A training penalty would encourage certain predictions, whereas a projection is an operation on the flux predictions. The proposal does not specify the projection algorithm or whether training also uses a conservation-related penalty.
So the network's initial phase-flux predictions do not have to be assumed conservative?

Correct. The reason for including a projection is to place the predicted fluxes under finite-volume continuity constraints afterward. That does not establish, in advance, how large any correction would be or what mass-balance error the resulting surrogate would achieve.
What is the finite-volume part referring to here?

It identifies the kind of continuity constraints used for the flux projection: fluxes must be consistent with a finite-volume accounting of flow through cells. That connects the proposal to the goal of local mass conservation. It does not mean the graph network itself is a finite-volume solver, or that projecting fluxes alone has already demonstrated the required cellwise error limit.
Does predicting saturation increments create a consistency question after the fluxes are projected?

Yes, conceptually. If the flux predictions change during projection, one would want to understand how the saturation increments relate to the fluxes that remain afterward. The proposal states that increments are predicted and fluxes are projected, but it does not specify a reconciliation rule. It would be premature to say that consistency is either guaranteed or violated.
Could you spell out the order without assuming extra steps?

First, train a transmissibility-aware graph network to predict phase fluxes and saturation increments. Then project the predicted fluxes onto finite-volume continuity constraints. That is the stated sequence. It does not prescribe an additional correction to saturation increments, a particular projection technique, or any further solver stage.
How does this proposal relate to the two numerical targets we discussed?

The flux projection is directed at the local-conservation side of the goal, whose requirement is a maximum cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. The transmissibility-aware predictions are intended for a surrogate that must also generalize across unseen permeability connectivity; on unseen channel connectivity, the breakthrough-time error must remain below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver. The proposed method is a way to pursue those targets, not evidence that either threshold has been met.
Does meeting the finite-volume continuity constraints automatically settle the breakthrough-time comparison?

No. The projection addresses continuity of the fluxes, while the breakthrough-time requirement tests predictive behavior on unseen channel connectivity against a converged finite-volume solver. A continuity-constrained prediction could still have breakthrough-time error above 5%. The comparison remains a separate requirement.
And I should not say that the projection alone proves the 0.1% cellwise limit?

Right. The proposal says to project fluxes onto finite-volume continuity constraints, but it does not report a measured maximum cellwise mass-balance error. In particular, it does not establish that the error stays below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. That numerical requirement would still need to be checked for the surrogate.
Is there a particular graph architecture or projection formula implied by this wording?

No specific architecture, formula, or training setup is given. “Transmissibility-aware graph network” identifies the type of predictive model and information it should account for; “project fluxes onto finite-volume continuity constraints” identifies the subsequent constraint operation. The details of either remain open in this proposal.
Then the essential distinction is learned predictions for phase fluxes and saturation increments, followed by an explicit continuity constraint on the fluxes?

Yes. The learned model predicts both quantities, and the stated post-prediction operation applies to the phase fluxes. Keeping those roles distinct preserves what the proposal actually specifies without assuming how saturation increments are handled after projection or claiming that the conservation and breakthrough-time targets are already satisfied.
How can predicted phase fluxes satisfy cellwise continuity without distorting breakthrough timing on unseen channel connectivity?

That is the central tension in the proposal. Projecting the predicted phase fluxes onto finite-volume continuity constraints can make the fluxes consistent with the specified cellwise accounting. But breakthrough timing depends on how flow moves through connected paths, so satisfying continuity alone does not ensure that the timing is preserved. The open question is whether the constrained fluxes remain faithful to the transport behavior the surrogate is trying to predict.
Why might a continuity correction affect breakthrough if it makes the fluxes more consistent?

Continuity constrains the balance at each cell; it does not, by itself, determine the correct distribution of flow among connected cells. A change to fluxes that fixes a local imbalance could also change how quickly a phase moves along a path. Thus a conservation improvement and a change in predicted breakthrough time can occur together, without either outcome establishing the other.
So is the issue that there could be more than one set of fluxes satisfying continuity?

Conceptually, yes. Meeting cellwise continuity is a constraint on the fluxes, not a complete description of which flux pattern best represents the two-phase flow. The projection must produce fluxes that satisfy the constraints, while the breakthrough-time requirement depends on whether those fluxes also represent transport accurately on unseen channel connectivity. The proposal does not specify how the projection chooses among possible constrained fluxes.
Would it be enough to make the correction small?

Keeping a correction from unnecessarily changing the predicted transport is a useful way to frame the concern, but a small correction alone would not guarantee an accurate breakthrough time. Its effect depends on what changes and where those changes occur. Likewise, the proposal has not specified a measure of correction size or established that the projection will be small.
Is unseen channel connectivity what makes this especially difficult to judge?

It is an important part of the question. The surrogate is meant to generalize across permeability connectivity it has not seen, and the breakthrough-time requirement specifically concerns unseen channel connectivity. A projection may enforce the same form of cellwise constraint there, but that does not tell us whether the network’s flux predictions—or the fluxes after projection—capture the resulting flow paths accurately.
Could I treat continuity as the first requirement and assume breakthrough timing follows from it?

No. Cellwise continuity addresses whether the fluxes respect the finite-volume balance constraints. Breakthrough timing addresses the predicted arrival behavior relative to the converged finite-volume solver on unseen channel connectivity. They are related through the flow prediction, but neither requirement is a substitute for the other.
The network also predicts saturation increments. Do they matter to this question?

They matter conceptually because saturation changes and phase fluxes are related parts of a two-phase flow prediction. If the fluxes are altered by projection, the relationship between the resulting fluxes and the predicted saturation increments becomes relevant. The proposal specifies a projection of the fluxes, but does not say whether or how the increments are adjusted, so it does not resolve that consistency question.
Does projecting the phase fluxes mean their cellwise continuity is guaranteed?

If the projection enforces the specified finite-volume continuity constraints as intended, its output satisfies those constraints by construction. That conditional statement does not establish a measured maximum cellwise mass-balance error for the full surrogate, nor does it establish that breakthrough timing is unaffected. Those depend on what the specified constraints cover and on the resulting prediction.
What should I avoid claiming when describing this approach?

Avoid claiming that a continuity projection automatically preserves breakthrough time, or that a transmissibility-aware prediction automatically generalizes to unseen channel connectivity. Also avoid claiming that the numerical conservation and breakthrough-time targets have been achieved: no resulting errors are given. At this point, the question is how to obtain both properties together, not a report that the proposal has already done so.
Can you put the unresolved issue in one sentence?
Can the predicted phase fluxes be brought into cellwise finite-volume continuity while retaining a flow pattern that predicts breakthrough time accurately on unseen channel connectivity?
My hypothesis is that a transmissibility-weighted flux projection will keep the peak cellwise residual below 0.1% of step injection and the breakthrough-time error on unseen connectivity below 5%.

That is a hypothesis about achieving both outcomes together, not a result yet. The projection is expected to keep the largest cellwise residual below 0.1% of the mass injected in a timestep, while keeping breakthrough-time error on unseen connectivity below 5% relative to the converged finite-volume solver. It directly addresses the concern that enforcing continuity might change breakthrough timing.
What is the significance of making the projection transmissibility-weighted?

It makes transmissibility relevant to how the flux projection is performed, rather than treating all flux adjustments as equivalent regardless of the flow connections. The hypothesis is that this will help satisfy the cellwise balance requirement without losing the transport behavior needed for accurate breakthrough timing. It does not specify a weighting formula or guarantee that either threshold will be met.
Does the weighting tell us which particular fluxes will change most?

Not from the hypothesis alone. “Transmissibility-weighted” identifies a factor used in the projection, but no precise rule is given for how it affects each adjustment. In particular, the wording does not say that fluxes on high-transmissibility connections must change more or less than others.
When I say “peak cellwise residual,” am I talking about the worst cell rather than the average?

Yes. “Peak cellwise residual” refers to the largest cellwise residual under consideration. The hypothesized limit is below 0.1% of step injection for that peak, not merely for an average across cells. Step injection here is the injected mass for the timestep used as the reference quantity.
Is “below 0.1%” meant as a strict threshold?

Yes. As worded, the hypothesis is that the peak residual stays below 0.1% of step injection, not merely equal to it. The breakthrough-time error is likewise hypothesized to stay below 5%, not at or below 5%.
The other part refers to unseen connectivity. Should I understand that as the same generalization concern about channel connectivity?

Yes. The goal concerns unseen permeability connectivity, with breakthrough-time accuracy specified on unseen channel connectivity. The hypothesis says the breakthrough error on unseen connectivity will stay below 5%. It should not be recast as a claim limited to connectivity already seen by the surrogate.
Does the projection itself make that breakthrough claim certain?

No. A projection can constrain flux balance without necessarily preserving the particular flow pattern that determines breakthrough timing. The transmissibility-weighted projection is hypothesized to meet both thresholds, but its effect on unseen-connectivity breakthrough remains part of what the hypothesis asserts, not something established by the word “projection.”
Could the residual be under the limit while breakthrough error is above 5%?

That is conceptually possible. The peak cellwise residual and breakthrough-time error measure different properties of the prediction. The hypothesis is stronger than either property alone: it says the transmissibility-weighted projection will keep both the peak residual below 0.1% of step injection and unseen-connectivity breakthrough-time error below 5%.
And accurate breakthrough timing by itself would not demonstrate the residual limit?

Correct. Breakthrough timing could be close to the converged finite-volume solver result without establishing that the largest cellwise residual is below 0.1% of step injection. Both parts of the hypothesis have their own numerical threshold.
Is the finite-volume solver the reference for the 0.1% figure as well?

No. The 0.1% residual limit is expressed relative to step injection. The converged finite-volume solver is the comparison baseline for breakthrough-time error on unseen channel connectivity. Those reference quantities should remain distinct.
Does a residual below 0.1% mean the projected fluxes have exactly zero continuity error?

Not necessarily. A strict bound below 0.1% of step injection permits a nonzero residual below that bound. The hypothesis states a numerical limit for the peak cellwise residual; it does not assert exact zero error.
Am I specifying a particular way to reconcile the predicted saturation increments with the projected fluxes?

No. The proposal includes network predictions of phase fluxes and saturation increments, followed by projection of the fluxes. This hypothesis specifies transmissibility weighting and the two expected error limits, but it does not add a rule for changing saturation increments after projection.
Would it be accurate to say the weighting is intended to address the tension between conservation and timing, without claiming it has done so?

Yes. The hypothesized role of transmissibility-weighted flux projection is to keep the peak cellwise residual below 0.1% of step injection without pushing unseen-connectivity breakthrough-time error to 5% or higher relative to the converged finite-volume solver. That states the intended joint outcome while leaving its success unproven.
What would be an overstatement of the hypothesis?

Saying the projection has already achieved either numerical limit would be an overstatement. So would saying that transmissibility weighting necessarily prevents breakthrough distortion or ensures exact conservation. The claim here is a testable expectation about both thresholds, not a reported measurement or a guarantee.
I want to benchmark the flux projection on 200 held-out channel topologies against converged finite volumes, measuring peak cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error.

That benchmark would evaluate the projection where the generalization question matters: on 200 channel topologies held out from the surrogate’s experience. It would record two separate outcomes—peak cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error—using converged finite-volume results for the comparison. This is an evaluation activity, not a report of results.
Why use held-out channel topologies rather than just checking the projected fluxes on familiar channels?

Because the question includes performance on unseen channel connectivity. Testing 200 held-out channel topologies makes the benchmark relevant to that condition. A check confined to familiar connectivity would not answer how the projection behaves on those held-out topologies.
What does the peak cellwise mass residual tell me here?

It focuses on the largest local mass-balance residual among the cells under evaluation. That matters because a small overall or average imbalance could coexist with a larger error in one cell. Measuring the peak lets the benchmark address the local-conservation aspect directly, without assuming that projecting fluxes has already achieved the intended limit.
And breakthrough-time error captures a different concern?

Yes. It asks how far the predicted breakthrough time is from the converged finite-volume result on held-out channel topologies. A projection might improve cellwise balance yet alter transport timing, so the benchmark measures timing as well as the local residual. Neither measurement can stand in for the other.
When I say ‘against converged finite volumes,’ am I specifying the comparison reference?

Yes. Converged finite-volume results are the stated benchmark reference. In particular, they provide the reference breakthrough time for assessing breakthrough-time error. The peak cellwise mass residual remains a local balance measurement; it should not be described merely as a difference between two breakthrough times.
Does the number 200 refer to cells or flow timesteps?
Neither. The activity specifies 200 held-out channel topologies. It does not state the number of cells, timesteps, or predictions within each topology.
Can I already say that the projection keeps the peak residual below 0.1% of step injection and breakthrough-time error below 5%?

Not on the basis of this activity statement. Those are the hypothesized limits the benchmark is meant to examine. No measured residuals or breakthrough-time errors have been supplied, so the activity cannot yet establish whether either limit holds across the 200 held-out channel topologies.
Would measuring only breakthrough-time error be enough to evaluate the hypothesis?

No. It would leave the peak cellwise mass residual unmeasured. The hypothesis concerns both local balance and breakthrough timing on unseen connectivity, which is why the benchmark explicitly includes both measurements.
What if I measured only peak cellwise mass residual?

That would leave the timing concern unanswered. Even if the flux projection produced a small local residual, the benchmark would still need breakthrough-time error against converged finite volumes to assess whether timing on held-out channel topologies was preserved.
Does ‘held-out’ itself tell us what the errors will be?

No. It describes the evaluation condition: those 200 channel topologies are held out. It does not imply that generalization succeeds or fails, or that the projection changes the fluxes by any particular amount.
Am I also proposing a separate comparison with predictions made without projection?

Not in this activity as stated. It specifies benchmarking the flux projection on 200 held-out channel topologies against converged finite volumes and measuring the two named errors. It does not specify an additional unprojected comparison.
What is the narrow conclusion this benchmark could eventually support?

Once the measurements exist, they could show how the flux projection performs on those 200 held-out channel topologies with respect to peak cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error against converged finite volumes. Whether the hypothesized numerical limits are satisfied would depend on those measurements; the benchmark plan alone does not settle it.
The benchmark results are in. Across 200 held-out channel topologies, the peak cellwise mass residual was 0.06% of timestep injection, and the maximum breakthrough-time error was 4.7%.

Those are the two reported measurements from the held-out benchmark. The 0.06% figure is the peak cellwise mass residual, expressed relative to the mass injected in a timestep. The 4.7% figure is the maximum breakthrough-time error, with converged finite-volume results providing the comparison for breakthrough time.
Does “peak cellwise” mean 0.06% is an average over the cells?
No. It identifies the largest reported cellwise mass residual across the benchmark, not an average over cells. The result does not give the residual for each individual cell.
And is 4.7% the average breakthrough-time error over the 200 topologies?
No. It is the maximum reported breakthrough-time error across the 200 held-out channel topologies. The result does not specify the average or the error for each topology.
I want to keep the reference quantities straight. What is each percentage relative to?

The 0.06% cellwise residual is relative to timestep injection. The 4.7% breakthrough-time error concerns breakthrough timing compared with the converged finite-volume results. They are percentages of different reference quantities and should not be treated as the same kind of error.
Can I describe the 0.06% residual as zero continuity error?
No. A reported peak residual of 0.06% of timestep injection is not zero. It gives the magnitude of the largest reported local residual under that normalization.
What does the number 200 count in this result?
It counts the held-out channel topologies in the benchmark. It is not a count of cells or timesteps, and the result does not provide those counts.
Does “held-out” matter when stating the result?

Yes. It identifies the connectivity condition under which these measurements were obtained. The figures are reported across 200 held-out channel topologies, rather than being presented without any stated evaluation setting.
Can these two numbers tell us how much the projection changed each predicted phase flux?
No. They report a peak cellwise mass residual and a maximum breakthrough-time error. They do not provide the individual predicted or projected phase fluxes, or the size of each projection adjustment.
What about the saturation increments predicted by the network?
These results do not report saturation-increment errors or describe any adjustment to those predictions. The two measurements given here concern cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error.
Can I infer that every possible unseen channel topology would have the same bounds as these 200?
No. The reported extrema describe the 200 held-out channel topologies that were benchmarked. They do not establish the errors for every possible unseen channel topology.
Then how should I state the finding without overstating its scope?

Across 200 held-out channel topologies in the flux-projection benchmark, the peak cellwise mass residual was 0.06% of timestep injection, and the maximum breakthrough-time error was 4.7% against converged finite-volume results. That states the measurements and their evaluation setting without extending them beyond the benchmark.
I’ve decided to retain the transmissibility-weighted projection. Both held-out worst-case metrics meet the acceptance limits, although the breakthrough-time error is nearing 5%.

That states both the decision and its qualification. The transmissibility-weighted projection is retained because the worst-case cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error on the held-out benchmark both meet their respective acceptance limits. The breakthrough-time error’s proximity to 5% is worth noting, but it does not change the stated decision.
What exactly does “both metrics” refer to here?

The peak cellwise mass residual and the maximum breakthrough-time error. The first is assessed against the limit below 0.1% of timestep injection; the second against the limit below 5% relative to converged finite-volume results on unseen channel connectivity. The decision rests on both held-out worst-case measurements meeting those limits.
Does “worst-case” mean I am relying on the largest observed errors rather than averages?

Yes. For this decision, the relevant held-out figures are the peak cellwise residual and the maximum breakthrough-time error. Saying those worst-case metrics meet the limits is different from saying only the averages meet them.
If breakthrough error is nearing 5%, why retain the projection?

Because the stated acceptance limit is below 5%, and the held-out worst-case breakthrough-time error meets it. The other worst-case metric—the peak cellwise mass residual—also meets its limit. The decision acknowledges that timing is close to its boundary without treating closeness as a failure of the stated criterion.
Should I call the breakthrough result comfortably below the limit?
No. “Nearing 5%” conveys a narrow margin relative to that limit. You can say it meets the limit, but describing it as comfortably below would lose the qualification included in the decision.
Does the narrow timing margin undermine the conservation part of the decision?

It does not change the stated finding that the held-out peak cellwise mass residual meets its acceptance limit. The two metrics address different properties. The timing qualification should remain attached to breakthrough-time error rather than being recast as a mass-balance failure.
Am I deciding to retain the whole surrogate unchanged?

The decision specifically says to retain the transmissibility-weighted projection. It does not separately decide that every part of the surrogate is unchanged or specify any other implementation choices.
Does this say the projection is the only possible way to satisfy the requirements?

No. Retaining this projection because its held-out worst-case metrics meet the acceptance limits is not a comparison establishing that no other approach could meet them. The decision concerns this projection and the stated reason for keeping it.
Can I say the decision proves performance on every unseen permeability connectivity?

No. Its stated basis is the held-out benchmark, which covered 200 channel topologies. The decision can refer to the worst-case metrics there meeting the acceptance limits, but it should not turn that into a guarantee for every possible unseen connectivity.
Is “retain despite breakthrough error nearing 5%” a fair short formulation?

Yes, provided the reason remains clear: retain the transmissibility-weighted projection because both held-out worst-case metrics meet their acceptance limits, despite the breakthrough-time error nearing the 5% limit. The qualification matters, but so does the fact that both criteria are met in the stated held-out evaluation.
Does retaining it mean the breakthrough-time error no longer matters?

No. Breakthrough-time error is one of the two metrics supporting the decision, and its proximity to 5% is explicitly part of the decision’s wording. Retaining the projection does not erase that narrow margin.
And meeting the two limits is the reason for the decision, not a claim of exact conservation or exact breakthrough timing?

Correct. The reason is that both held-out worst-case metrics meet their acceptance limits. That does not mean cellwise residual is zero or breakthrough-time error is zero; in particular, breakthrough-time error is described as nearing 5%.

Using the retained transmissibility-weighted projection, I plan to train with rewired channels. Then I’ll compare peak cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error against finite-volume results on independent topologies.

That keeps the retained projection in the surrogate while using rewired channels for training. The subsequent comparison on independent topologies addresses two distinct questions: how large the worst local mass-balance residual is, and how accurately the surrogate predicts breakthrough time relative to finite volumes. This is a plan for training and evaluation, not a report of results from the independent topologies.
What is the purpose of training with rewired channels in this plan?

It puts variation in channel connectivity into the training activity, in keeping with the goal of generalizing across unseen permeability connectivity. The plan does not specify how channels are rewired, how many rewired examples are used, or what effect that training will have on accuracy.
Do the independent topologies play the same role as the rewired channels used for training?

They have different stated roles. Rewired channels are part of the planned training, while independent topologies are where the planned comparison will take place. Keeping those roles separate is important to the generalization question; the plan does not specify how the independent topologies are generated.
Why compare both peak cellwise residual and breakthrough-time error again?

Because they address different parts of the surrogate’s goal. Peak cellwise mass residual checks the largest local mass-balance discrepancy, whereas breakthrough-time error checks transport timing against the finite-volume reference. Training with rewired channels could affect either measure, so the plan calls for comparing both on independent topologies rather than treating one as a proxy for the other.
Does “peak cellwise” mean I could just report an average residual across cells?
No. The peak is the largest cellwise residual under the comparison. An average could conceal a larger discrepancy in a particular cell, so it would not express the planned peak measurement.
What reference should I keep in mind for that residual?

The goal expresses the cellwise mass-balance limit as below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. The plan says to compare peak cellwise residual on independent topologies, but it does not give a new residual value or a different normalization. The finite-volume comparison should not be confused with the injected-mass reference for that percentage limit.
And how should I understand the breakthrough comparison against finite volumes?

It concerns the difference between the surrogate’s predicted breakthrough time and the finite-volume result on the independent topologies. For the goal’s numerical criterion on unseen channel connectivity, the reference is a converged finite-volume solver and the error must remain below 5%. The plan does not yet say what the error will be.
Does the plan assume that rewiring during training will prevent the projection from shifting breakthrough timing?

No. Training with rewired channels and retaining the projection are planned choices. Comparing breakthrough-time error on independent topologies is how the plan examines timing; the wording does not establish in advance whether timing is preserved or distorted.
Should the projected fluxes still be considered when I interpret the residual?

Yes. The plan explicitly uses the retained projection, so the peak cellwise residual being compared concerns the resulting surrogate with that projection in use. But the plan does not specify the projection’s adjustments or provide a residual measurement for the independent topologies.
Am I proposing another benchmark on exactly 200 topologies?

No number of independent topologies is specified in this plan. It says to compare the two metrics on independent topologies, without setting their count or saying they are the same topologies used in any other evaluation.
Does ‘independent’ by itself guarantee that they cover every kind of unseen channel connectivity?

No. It identifies the intended separation of the comparison topologies from the training activity, but it does not describe their range or guarantee coverage of every possible connectivity. The planned measurements would speak to the independent topologies actually compared.
Could I present the training with rewired channels as already completed?

Not from this node. The activity is stated as a plan: train with rewired channels using the retained projection, then compare peak cellwise residual and breakthrough-time error against finite volumes on independent topologies. It supplies no completed training outcome or comparison results.
Is there an additional architecture change in the plan?

None is specified. The plan identifies the retained projection, training with rewired channels, and the two comparisons on independent topologies. It does not prescribe a new graph architecture, a rewiring procedure, or a change to how saturation increments are handled.
So the comparison is intended to check conservation and timing under a separate connectivity evaluation, without presuming either result?

Exactly. With the retained projection in use, the plan is to train with rewired channels and evaluate peak cellwise mass residual and breakthrough-time error against finite volumes on independent topologies. Those measurements would address local conservation and breakthrough timing under that evaluation condition; the plan itself makes no claim that either numerical target has been reached there.

I’m moving to the training and scoring activity: train the projected graph surrogate on 10,000 rewired-channel cases, then score mass residual and breakthrough-time error on 100 independent finite-volume simulations.

That specifies the two parts of the activity and their sizes. The projected graph surrogate is trained on 10,000 rewired-channel cases. Mass residual and breakthrough-time error are then scored using 100 independent finite-volume simulations. No scores or conclusions about the numerical limits are stated yet.
Which number belongs to training, and which belongs to evaluation?

The 10,000 rewired-channel cases belong to training. The 100 independent finite-volume simulations belong to scoring. The activity does not say that 100 of the training cases are reused for that evaluation.
Do the 100 simulations mean there are exactly 100 independent topologies?

Not necessarily. The activity counts 100 independent finite-volume simulations; it does not specify a one-to-one relationship between simulations and distinct topologies. The broader plan calls for comparison on independent topologies, but the number given here is a number of simulations.
What does “projected” identify in the graph surrogate?

It identifies the graph surrogate used with the flux projection discussed earlier. The model predicts flow-related quantities, and its predicted phase fluxes are projected onto finite-volume continuity constraints. This activity does not introduce a different projection method or specify additional implementation details.
Is the projection something being scored separately from the surrogate?
